title: What is Christianity?
q: What do Christians believe, and how does that shape the way they live?

b.x: Welcome. This is the first of two preparatory lessons before we begin the full course. Tonight we look at what Christianity is about: what Christians believe, what the Bible is, and what the Christian life looks like.
When you hear the word Christianity, what comes to mind?
Let people share freely. There are no wrong answers here.
Father, thank You for bringing us together. Open our minds and hearts tonight as we learn about You and Your plan for us. In Jesus' name, amen.

Christianity is built on the life and teachings of Jesus Christ. It is the most widely followed faith in the world, and it rests on a set of beliefs that have held firm for over two thousand years. Let us walk through the core beliefs together.
Core beliefs
Christians believe in one eternal God who created the universe and all life. God exists in three persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus Christ), and the Holy Spirit. This is called the Trinity.
Every person has sinned and is separated from God. We cannot fix this on our own. That is why God sent Jesus.
Romans 3:23
Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was born of the Virgin Mary. He lived a sinless life, died on the cross to pay for our sins, and rose bodily from the dead on the third day. He is alive today.
1 Corinthians 15:3-4
Salvation comes by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone. No one earns it by good works or personal effort.
Ephesians 2:8-9
One day Jesus will return to judge the living and the dead and to establish His eternal kingdom.
The Bible
The Bible is the inspired Word of God. It has two main sections: the Old Testament and the New Testament.
The Old Testament records how God dealt with His people Israel. It includes history, wisdom writings, poetry, and prophecies about the coming Messiah.

The New Testament centers on Jesus. The four Gospels record His life, death, and resurrection. The book of Acts tells how the early church grew. The letters (also called Epistles) explain Christian teaching and daily living. Revelation describes the return of Christ and the end of the age.
2 Timothy 3:16-17
All Scripture is given by God and is useful for teaching, correcting, and training us in how to live right.
The Christian life
True Christianity is more than a set of beliefs. It is a way of life. Christians seek to trust and follow Jesus every day, being transformed by the power of the Holy Spirit.

This involves repenting of sin and placing faith in Jesus. It means being baptized as a public testimony. It means practicing spiritual disciplines like prayer, worship, and Bible study. It means living by the principles of love, integrity, purity, and service.
Christians serve God with their time, talents, and resources. They gather together with other believers in a local church. They share the good news of Jesus with others.
John 3:16
God loved the world so much that He gave His only Son. Everyone who believes in Him will not perish but will have eternal life. That is the heart of the Christian message.
What stands out to you the most from what we covered tonight?
Why do you think the Bible is important for Christians?
What part of living as a Christian seems most challenging to you? What part seems exciting?
Next time we will talk about how spiritual growth begins and what to expect in this course. Thank you for being here. Let us close in prayer.
Lord, thank You for what we learned tonight. Help each one of us to keep thinking about who You are and what You have done for us. Amen.

title: Basics of Spiritual Growth
q: How does a person begin and grow in the Christian life?

b.x: Welcome back. Last time we talked about what Christianity is. Tonight we look at how the Christian life begins, the habits that help us grow, and what to expect in the lessons ahead.
Since last week, did anything from our first lesson stay with you?
Give people time. Affirm whatever they share.
Father, thank You for each person here tonight. Help us understand what it means to grow closer to You. In Jesus' name, amen.
Beginning the Christian life
The Christian life begins with a personal decision to receive Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. This involves three things.
First, admitting your need. Everyone has sinned and fallen short of God's standard. We cannot save ourselves.
Romans 3:23
Second, believing in Jesus. We trust that He died for our sins, rose again, and is the only way to God.
John 14:6
Third, confessing your faith. We declare openly that Jesus is Lord.
Romans 10:9
If you declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.
Baptism is an important next step. It is a public act that identifies you with Christ. It shows the world that your old life is behind you and your new life has begun.
Spiritual disciplines
Spiritual disciplines are habits that help us grow in Christlikeness. Here are the core ones.

Bible study means reading, studying, and thinking deeply about God's Word. Prayer is personal communication with God. Worship is praising God and giving Him honor in all of life. Service is using your abilities to serve God and others. Fellowship is encouraging and building up other believers.
1 Timothy 4:7
Paul told Timothy to train himself to be godly. Consistency in these disciplines is what produces lasting growth.
The process of discipleship

Discipleship is the lifelong process of becoming more like Jesus. It involves instruction, where we learn biblical truth. Modeling, where we follow the example of mature believers. Practice, where we apply what we learn to daily life. Accountability, where we give and receive guidance and correction.
No Christian has arrived at perfection. We all stumble at times. The overall direction of a disciple's life, though, is one of growth in holiness and Christlike character.
Philippians 1:6
God who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. That is a promise.
What to expect in this course

In the lessons ahead you will explore key sections and themes of the Bible. You will examine the fundamentals of Christian teaching. You will learn how to develop a consistent walk with God. You will discover your spiritual gifts and learn to use them. You will prepare to share your faith and disciple others.
This is a journey. It takes time. Come with an open heart and a willingness to learn, and God will do the rest.
Have you made a personal commitment to follow Jesus Christ? If so, how did that happen?
Which spiritual discipline do you find most natural? Which one is most challenging?
What are you most looking forward to in the coming lessons?
Next week we begin the full course. Thank you for taking the time to prepare. Let us close in prayer.
Lord, thank You for this time together. Prepare our hearts for everything ahead. Help us grow in faith, in love, and in knowledge of You. In Jesus' name, amen.

title: Navigating the Bible
q: How is the Bible organized, and how do you find and study a passage?

b.x: Welcome. This is our third preparatory lesson. Tonight we learn how the Bible is put together, how to find any passage, and how to begin studying it on your own.
Have you ever tried to look something up in the Bible? What was that experience like?
Let people share freely. Some may never have opened a Bible before.
Father, thank You for giving us Your Word. Help us tonight to understand how it is arranged so we can find and learn from it more easily. In Jesus' name, amen.
The Bible is not just one book. It is a collection of 66 books written by about 40 authors over 1,500 years. It is divided into two main sections: the Old Testament and the New Testament.
The Old Testament

The Old Testament has 39 books. They are grouped into five categories: the Law (Genesis through Deuteronomy), History (Joshua through Esther), Poetry and Wisdom (Job through Song of Solomon), the Major Prophets (Isaiah through Daniel), and the Minor Prophets (Hosea through Malachi).
The Old Testament records how God created the world, chose the nation of Israel, gave them His law, and promised to send a Savior.
The New Testament

The New Testament has 27 books. The four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John) tell the story of Jesus. Acts records how the early church grew. The letters of Paul and other apostles explain Christian teaching and daily living. Revelation describes the return of Christ and the end of the age.
2 Timothy 3:16-17
All Scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, correcting, and training in righteousness. That includes every part of both Testaments.
Finding a passage

Bible references follow a simple pattern: book name, chapter number, then verse number. For example, John 3:16 means the book of John, chapter 3, verse 16. A dash shows a range of verses: Ephesians 2:8-10 means chapter 2, verses 8 through 10.
Most Bibles have a table of contents in the front. Use it until you learn where each book falls. With practice, you will find passages quickly.
Psalm 119:105
Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. The more familiar you become with the Bible, the more it lights your way.
Choosing a translation

The Bible was originally written in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek. Today it has been translated into many languages. Some translations follow the original words closely, like the ESV, NASB, and NKJV. Others focus on making the thought easy to understand, like the NIV, NLT, and CSB.
For study, a translation closer to the original words is helpful. For daily reading, an easier version works well. Many people use more than one.
How to study the Bible

Here are simple steps you can follow. Begin with prayer, asking God to help you understand. Read the passage in context, not just one verse by itself. Look for the main idea and any repeated words. Write down what you notice and any questions you have. Use a study Bible or commentary if you want to go deeper. Most importantly, look for something you can apply to your own life.
Joshua 1:8
God told Joshua to meditate on His Word day and night. The goal of Bible study is not just knowledge. It is to know God and be changed by what He says.
Have you ever tried to read the Bible on your own? What was your experience?
Which part of the Bible's structure was new to you tonight? What questions do you still have?
What practical step can you take this week to begin reading the Bible more regularly?
You now know how the Bible is arranged, how to find a passage, and how to begin studying it. Next time we start the full course. Thank you for being here. Let us close in prayer.
Lord, thank You for Your Word. Help each of us to open it this week and begin to hear Your voice through it. In Jesus' name, amen.
